studies.Reference: Bacterial Vaginosis-Associated Bacteria and Uterine Fibroids: A Nested Case-Control Study.
studies.Authors: Moore KR, Tomar M, Umbach DM, Gygax SE, Hilbert DW, Baird DD
studies.comparison_type: Only BV-associated bacteria, no optimal Lactobacillus bacteria vs optimal Lactobacillus
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: We used quantitative polymerase chain reaction, an objective molecular method, to assess 9 BV-associated and 4 Lactobacillus species from vaginal swab specimens.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: nested case-control study of 200 women (100 cases and 100 controls)
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: High imbalance (only BV-associated bacteria, no optimal Lactobacillus bacteria) was actually inversely associated with fibroid incidence (odds ratio, 0.38; 95% confidence interval, 0.17-0.81).
extraction_supporting_text.outcome_definition: incident fibroids with standardized ultrasound examinations
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: 4 Lactobacillus species from vaginal swab specimens

studies.Reference: Cervical Microbiota Associated with Higher Grade Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia in Women Infected with High-Risk Human Papillomaviruses.
studies.Authors: Piyathilake CJ, Ollberding NJ, Kumar R, Macaluso M, Alvarez RD, Morrow CD
studies.comparison_type: Lactobacillus-dominated cervical mucosal community type (CT) vs other CTs
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Microbiota composition was determined by Illumina sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene amplified from DNA extracted from cervical mucus samples.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: The study included 340 women diagnosed with CIN 2+ (cases) and 90 diagnosed with CIN 1 (non-cases).
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: a cervical mucosal community type (CT) dominated by L. iners and unclassified Lactobacillus spp was associated with CIN 2+ (OR = 3.48; 95% CI, 1.27-9.55)
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: cervical mucosal community type (CT) dominated by L. iners and unclassified Lactobacillus spp

headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger's test indicates no significant funnel plot asymmetry (p=0.4746). The distribution of studies appears symmetric, suggesting a lower risk of publication bias.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 4 studies yielded an effect size of 1.35 (95% CI: 0.6–3.05), indicating no statistically significant association between lactobacillus and uterine cancer. Although the point estimate suggests a potential positive relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by very high heterogeneity (I² = 90.63%), reflecting highly inconsistent results across studies.
